questions.title: Statement that is NOT true of lipoprotein lipase
questions.question: All the following about lipoprotein lipase are correct EXCEPT:

options.A: It is present in the endothelial cells of extrahepatic tissue
options.B: Its synthesis is decreased by insulin, and heparin stimulates its release
options.C: It requires the cofactors phospholipids and apo C-II
options.D: Deficiency of lipoprotein lipase leads to type I hyperlipoproteinaemia

explanations.A: Incorrect as the answer. Lipoprotein lipase is indeed anchored to the luminal surface of capillary endothelial cells of extrahepatic tissues (adipose, muscle, lactating mammary gland).
explanations.B: Correct. This is the false statement. Insulin INCREASES, not decreases, lipoprotein lipase synthesis (notably in adipose tissue after a meal). The heparin clause is true (heparin releases the enzyme from the endothelium into plasma), but because the insulin clause is wrong the whole statement is incorrect, making it the exception.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the answer. Lipoprotein lipase genuinely requires apo C-II (supplied by circulating lipoproteins) as an activator and phospholipid for its action.
explanations.D: Incorrect as the answer. Lipoprotein lipase deficiency (or apo C-II deficiency) does cause type I hyperlipoproteinaemia, with fasting chylomicronaemia.

questions.title: Enzyme class of pancreatic lipase
questions.question: Pancreatic lipase, which hydrolyses fats, acts as a:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Peptidases hydrolyse peptide bonds in proteins; pancreatic lipase acts on ester bonds in triacylglycerol, not on peptides.
explanations.B: Correct. Pancreatic lipase hydrolyses the ester bonds of triacylglycerol (removing fatty acids from positions 1 and 3 to give 2-monoacylglycerol and free fatty acids). Adding water to cleave a bond makes it a hydrolase.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Carboxylases add a carboxyl (CO2) group and require biotin; lipase neither adds CO2 nor uses biotin.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Dehydrogenases catalyse oxidation-reduction by transferring hydrogen/electrons, which is not what lipase does.

questions.title: How L-amino acids are absorbed
questions.question: The L-amino acids are absorbed from the intestine by:

explanations.A: Correct. L-amino acids are absorbed across the enterocyte apical membrane mainly by secondary active transport, coupled to the inward sodium gradient (analogous to SGLT1 for glucose). This lets them be taken up against their concentration gradient.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Simple passive diffusion is negligible for the polar, charged amino acids and cannot move them against a gradient.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Pinocytosis of intact protein occurs only transiently in the neonatal gut (e.g. for immunoglobulins), not for routine L-amino-acid absorption in the adult.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Some minor carrier-mediated facilitated uptake exists, but the principal, defining mechanism for L-amino acids is sodium-dependent active transport.

questions.title: Amino acid not needed for glutathione synthesis
questions.question: Which of the following amino acids is NOT required for the synthesis of glutathione?

explanations.A: Correct. Glutathione is the tripeptide gamma-glutamyl-cysteinyl-glycine, built from glutamate, cysteine and glycine. Serine is not one of its constituent amino acids, so it is not required for its synthesis.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Cysteine is an essential constituent of glutathione and provides its reactive thiol (-SH) group.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Glutamic acid (glutamate) is the N-terminal residue, joined through its gamma-carboxyl in the unusual gamma-peptide bond.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Glycine is the C-terminal residue of the glutathione tripeptide.

questions.title: Reaction not belonging to phase I detoxification
questions.question: The major detoxification reactions involved in phase I are the following EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect as the answer. Reduction is a phase I reaction, introducing or exposing a functional group on the xenobiotic.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the answer. Oxidation (largely by cytochrome P450) is the archetypal phase I reaction.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the answer. Hydroxylation is a common cytochrome-P450-mediated phase I oxidation.
explanations.D: Correct. Methylation is a conjugation reaction of phase II, not phase I. Phase I comprises oxidation, reduction and hydrolysis (including hydroxylation) that unmask or add a reactive group; phase II then conjugates that group (methylation, sulfation, glucuronidation, acetylation, glutathione conjugation). Methylation therefore does not belong to phase I.

questions.title: Reaction not belonging to phase II detoxification
questions.question: The major detoxification reactions involved in phase II are the following EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect as the answer. Conjugation is the defining activity of phase II, attaching a polar group to increase water solubility for excretion.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the answer. Methylation is a phase II conjugation reaction (using S-adenosylmethionine).
explanations.C: Correct. Hydroxylation is a phase I reaction (cytochrome-P450 oxidation), not phase II. Phase II reactions are conjugations, methylation, sulfation, glucuronidation, acetylation and glutathione conjugation, so hydroxylation is the exception here.
explanations.D: Incorrect as the answer. Sulfation (sulfate conjugation) is a classic phase II reaction.
